A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FonTS and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and supplementary materials. Content can be matched across the extensive rearrangement of the appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original BTR, ATR, and MARIO-bench results, component ablations, and a user study involving 22 participants.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds image-adapter comparisons, AnyText experiments, and further typography and style-control ablations.

M1.justification: The ETC-token, Txt-Attn fine-tuning, and two-phase SCA pipeline and its equations remain. However, v1 Section 4 says CLIP text conditioning is omitted during TC-finetuning, whereas v2 specifies a fixed CLIP prompt. The PDFs do not resolve whether this changes conditioning or clarifies its earlier description. Newly specified alternating adapter placement alone does not establish an architectural change.

E1.justification: Both use the approximately 50k-image TC-Dataset, 580k-pair SC-general, and 20k-image SC-artext, alongside BTR-bench, ATR-bench, and MARIO-bench. The added experiments remain within the existing typography, artistic-text, and scene-text coverage.

E2.justification: v2 Table 3 adds evaluated SD3-IPA, Flux-IPA, and Flux-Redux competitors to the ATR comparison. Appendix A.4 and Table 11 add AnyText and TC-finetuned AnyText for BTR. Glyph-ByT5 and TextDiffuser-2 are retained under abbreviated names. The Midjourney comparison is retained as Figure 24, moved from v1 Figure 6.

E3.justification: v2 introduces FontCLIP-I for BTR and CLIP-I for ATR. ATR comparisons now evaluate image scales 0.9 and 0.6, simple versus style captions, and original versus interpolated Redux settings. New ablations introduce additional training-component and adapter-placement configurations. These substantially extend the evaluation design within the retained benchmarks.

E4.justification: v2 expands the training-module ablation with tokens-only and T5 fine-tuning, adds combined Art-FT/TC-FT tests and comparisons of adapter insertion sites, and examines generation without SCA. New attention maps investigate backbone differences. Existing ETC-token and language-drift analyses are retained, with additional ETC-token visual evidence.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 25 explicitly displays generation seeds 0–3 across T5 fine-tuning checkpoints, adding seed information beyond v1's fixed-seed style comparisons. Neither version reports confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates across repeated training runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds consistency scores, image-adapter results, and new ablation outcomes, including zero OCR accuracy for T5 fine-tuning. Txt-Attn and ETC-token ablation OCR changes from 81.43 to 82.85; shared main BTR and STR scores remain. The earlier single-/multi-word TC-FT breakdown is replaced by stage and placement analyses. ATR Style-Con changes from 74.43 to 31.82/34.09 under expanded comparisons and scale settings, preventing a direct performance-decline interpretation.

T1.justification: Equations 1–5, the conditional flow-matching objective, attention definitions, and parameter-change calculation are retained. The additional mechanism explanations introduce no new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or substantive mathematical derivations.

C1.justification: v2 newly claims that the existing TC-Dataset is the first word-level controllable dataset and makes this a separate contribution in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion. The central claims about word-level control, font/style consistency, and preservation of scene-text rendering remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for tokens-only/T5 failures, the complementary effects of Art-FT and TC-FT, and limited transfer of typography fine-tuning to AnyText. It also connects training length and overfitting to the absence of DPO and expands discussion of content leakage in image adapters. The existing language-drift limitation and cross-task transfer qualifications remain.

D1.justification: v2 specifies alternating SCA insertion at layers 0, 2, 4, and so on, 512-resolution training, and baseline implementation links. It reports total batches of 32/64, compatible with v1's 2/4 batches, eight GPUs, and two-step accumulation; a larger training budget is not established. DeepSpeed/accumulation details disappear, while a future academic release of datasets and models is promised.

R1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds a four-part positioning against Flux-IPA covering training stages, insertion sites, image encoders, and parameter cost. v2 also expands T5-versus-CLIP positioning and adds references including AnyDoor, FontCLIP, DINOv2, and SigLIP. Together with the new dataset-novelty claim, this substantially extends the comparative rationale beyond bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the abstract and contribution list, condenses related work, expands the token-design explanation, and moves style-training material from Experiments into Approach. Quantitative discussion is reorganized by task, and the retained supplementary material is extensively reordered around results and ablations.

P2.justification: v2 redesigns Figure 1, expands the style-comparison grid, splits the combined BTR/ATR table, and adds numerous ablation displays. The Midjourney comparison and scene-stylization examples move into the appendix, while dataset example figures are merged. These are substantial display and layout changes beyond numerical updates.

improvement.justification: v1's quantitative ATR comparison used text-only SD3/Flux competitors and provided limited evidence isolating SCA's design choices. v2 substantially addresses these weaknesses through image-conditioned competitors, caption/scale controls, automatic consistency metrics, and training-stage/placement ablations. Reporting remains imperfect: Table 3's OCR values 61.78/59.66 average 60.72, whereas Tables 6–7 report 60.07. This limits confidence in exact aggregates, but the comparative and component-level evidence supporting the central contributions improves substantially.
